examples.question_text: A particle's position in metres is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=3t^2\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^3+5t)\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t\geq0$ is measured in seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration vectors, then its velocity and speed at $t=1$.
examples.solution_text:
Differentiate each component separately.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=\dfrac{d}{dt}(3t^2)\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{d}{dt}(t^3+5t)\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=6t\underset{\sim}{i}+(3t^2+5)\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{a}(t)&=6\underset{\sim}{i}+6t\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$
Velocity is measured in metres per second and acceleration in metres per second squared.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(1)&=6\underset{\sim}{i}+8\underset{\sim}{j}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\\|\underset{\sim}{v}(1)|&=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}\\&=10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^{3t}\underset{\sim}{i}+\ln(2t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its velocity and acceleration vectors.
examples.solution_text:
Apply the chain rule to each component.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=3e^{3t}\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{2}{2t+1}\underset{\sim}{j}\\\underset{\sim}{a}(t)&=9e^{3t}\underset{\sim}{i}-\dfrac{4}{(2t+1)^2}\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=te^{-2t}\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^2+3)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its velocity at $t=0$.
examples.solution_text:
Use the product rule for the first component.
$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}(t)&=e^{-2t}-2te^{-2t}\\\dot{y}(t)&=2t\\\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=(e^{-2t}-2te^{-2t})\underset{\sim}{i}+2t\underset{\sim}{j}\\\underset{\sim}{v}(0)&=(1-0)\underset{\sim}{i}+0\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=\underset{\sim}{i}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\dfrac{2t}{t+2}\underset{\sim}{i}+\sqrt{6t+1}\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its velocity vector.
examples.solution_text:
Use the quotient rule for the first component and the chain rule for the second.
$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}(t)&=\dfrac{2(t+2)-2t}{(t+2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{4}{(t+2)^2}\\\dot{y}(t)&=\dfrac{6}{2\sqrt{6t+1}}\\&=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{6t+1}}\\\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=\dfrac{4}{(t+2)^2}\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{6t+1}}\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A particle's position in metres is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=3\cos(4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+3\sin(4t)\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t\geq0$ is measured in seconds and angles are in radians. Show that its speed is constant, that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=-16\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$, and that its velocity and acceleration are perpendicular.

A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t^3-9t^2)\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{t^4}{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find its acceleration vector and the time when the first component of acceleration is zero. Is the entire acceleration vector zero then?
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=(6t^2-18t)\underset{\sim}{i}+2t^3\underset{\sim}{j}\\\underset{\sim}{a}(t)&=(12t-18)\underset{\sim}{i}+6t^2\underset{\sim}{j}\end{aligned}$
Set the first component equal to zero.
$\begin{aligned}12t-18&=0\\12t&=18\\t&=\dfrac32\end{aligned}$
$\underset{\sim}{a}\left(\dfrac32\right)=\dfrac{27}{2}\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Only the first component is zero; the acceleration vector is non-zero.

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(2t^2+pt)\underset{\sim}{i}+qt^3\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Given $\underset{\sim}{v}(2)=11\underset{\sim}{i}+24\underset{\sim}{j}$, find $p$ and $q$.
A particle's position in metres is $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^2-6t)\underset{\sim}{i}+4t\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $t\geq0$ is measured in seconds. Find its minimum speed and when it occurs.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(t)&=(2t-6)\underset{\sim}{i}+4\underset{\sim}{j}\\|\underset{\sim}{v}(t)|^2&=(2t-6)^2+16\end{aligned}$
The square root is increasing, so minimise the squared speed. The squared term has minimum zero.
$\begin{aligned}2t-6&=0\\t&=3\end{aligned}$
This time is in the domain $t\geq0$.
$\begin{aligned}|\underset{\sim}{v}(3)|&=\sqrt{0+16}\\&=4\ \text{m s}^{-1}\end{aligned}$
The minimum speed is $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $t=3\ \text{s}$.

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^t\cos(2t)\underset{\sim}{i}+e^t\sin(2t)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Show that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=2\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-5\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.
examples.solution_text:
Differentiate using the product and chain rules.
$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}(t)&=e^t\cos(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t)\\\dot{y}(t)&=e^t\sin(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t)\\\ddot{x}(t)&=e^t\cos(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t)-4e^t\cos(2t)\\&=-3e^t\cos(2t)-4e^t\sin(2t)\\\ddot{y}(t)&=e^t\sin(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t)-4e^t\sin(2t)\\&=-3e^t\sin(2t)+4e^t\cos(2t)\end{aligned}$
Now compare components of the required expression.
$\begin{aligned}2\dot{x}(t)-5x(t)&=2(e^t\cos(2t)-2e^t\sin(2t))-5e^t\cos(2t)\\&=-3e^t\cos(2t)-4e^t\sin(2t)\\&=\ddot{x}(t)\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}2\dot{y}(t)-5y(t)&=2(e^t\sin(2t)+2e^t\cos(2t))-5e^t\sin(2t)\\&=-3e^t\sin(2t)+4e^t\cos(2t)\\&=\ddot{y}(t)\end{aligned}$
Both components agree, so $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=2\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-5\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$.

examples.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^2-10t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^2+4t)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\geq0$. Find when its velocity is parallel to $\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j}$.
examples.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=(2t-10)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t+4)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
For parallel vectors, the second component must be twice the first.
$\begin{aligned}2t+4&=2(2t-10)\\2t+4&=4t-20\\24&=2t\\t&=12\end{aligned}$
Check the velocity is a non-zero scalar multiple of the given vector.
$\begin{aligned}\underset{\sim}{v}(12)&=14\underset{\sim}{i}+28\underset{\sim}{j}\\&=14(\underset{\sim}{i}+2\underset{\sim}{j})\end{aligned}$
The required time is $t=12$.

examples.derivation: Component differentiation gives v(t)=(6t,3t²+5) and a(t)=(6,6t). Thus v(1)=(6,8) m/s and speed=√(36+64)=10 m/s. Acceleration units are m/s². No diagram is needed.
Differentiating gives v(t)=(3e^(3t),2/(2t+1)); differentiating again gives a(t)=(9e^(3t),−4/(2t+1)²). The logarithm and derivatives are defined throughout t≥0. No diagram is needed.
The product rule gives x′(t)=e^(−2t)(1−2t), while y′(t)=2t. Substitution after differentiation gives v(0)=(1,0)=i. No diagram is needed.
The quotient rule gives x′=[2(t+2)−2t]/(t+2)²=4/(t+2)². The chain rule gives y′=3/√(6t+1). Both components are defined for t≥0. No diagram is needed.

Writing θ=4t gives v=(−12sinθ,12cosθ), so |v|²=144 and speed=12 m/s. A second derivative gives a=(−48cosθ,−48sinθ)=−16r. Their dot product is 576sinθcosθ−576cosθsinθ=0; magnitudes 12 and 48 ensure both vectors are non-zero. At t=0, P=(3,0), velocity points upward and acceleration left towards O, matching the planar diagram. Direction-only arrows are explicitly identified; the circle is unshaded and ordinary labels specify black 10 pt text.

Differentiation gives v=(6t²−18t,2t³) and a=(12t−18,6t²). The first acceleration component vanishes at t=3/2. The second component then equals 6(9/4)=27/2, so the acceleration vector is non-zero. No diagram is needed.
Differentiating gives v=(4t+p,3qt²). At t=2, equating components yields 8+p=11 and 12q=24, hence p=3 and q=2. No diagram is needed.
Velocity is (2t−6,4), with squared speed (2t−6)²+16≥16. Equality occurs at t=3, within t≥0. Therefore the minimum speed is 4 m/s at 3 s. No diagram is needed.
Writing c=cos(2t) and s=sin(2t), differentiation gives v=e^t(c−2s,s+2c) and a=e^t(−3c−4s,−3s+4c). Independently, 2v−5r=e^t(−3c−4s,−3s+4c), proving the identity componentwise. No diagram is needed.
Velocity is (2t−10,2t+4). Parallelism to (1,2) requires 2t+4=2(2t−10), giving t=12. This is in the domain, and v(12)=(14,28)=14(1,2) is non-zero. No diagram is needed.
